
This vignette shows how to add altitude to the header table for `resy_classify()`. The elevation map is too large to be included in the package, so you need to download it separately.

Whether you need altitude depends on the expert system. In the
[EUNIS](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/123d0c9a-a6fa-4f2d-b887-5d8e5468faed)
expert system ([version 2025-10-03](https://zenodo.org/records/16895007)), for
example, 15 habitat types use altitude:
snow-bed vegetation (R41) and Iberian summer pasture (R24), alpine and
subalpine scrub (S21, S22, S23, S25, S26), dry heath (S42), mountain forests
(T1C, T1D, T31, T32, T34, T37) and coniferous plantations of non site-native
trees (T3M).

If your data already records altitude, in a column `Altitude (m)` or `Altitude`,
or as the Darwin Core columns `minimumElevationInMeters` and
`maximumElevationInMeters`, RESY uses it directly and you do not need this
vignette.

```{r libraries, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
```

## Example

The example uses a small part of the elevation map and the example plots that lie in it.

### Load data

Load the altitude data for the example area:

```{r example-data-altitude, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
altitude <- terra::rast(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_altitude.tif", package = "RESY")
)
altitude
```

Load the example plots that lie in this area:

```{r example-data-sites, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
data_sites <- readr::read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_sites.csv", package = "RESY"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::select(PlotObservationID, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(altitude)) |>
  sf::st_crop(sf::st_bbox(altitude)) # the example uses part of the map
```

The map shows the altitude and the example plots (red):

```{r map, message=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Elevation map of the example area, colored from low to high altitude, with the example plots shown as red points."}
ggplot() +
  tidyterra::geom_spatraster(data = altitude) +
  tidyterra::scale_fill_whitebox_c(
    palette = "high_relief",
    na.value = "lightblue"
    ) +
  geom_sf(data = data_sites, color = "red", size = 2) +
  labs(fill = "Altitude (m)") +
  theme_classic()
```

© EuroGeographics 2026, Istituto Geografico Militare (IGM), Italy; [Licence](https://www.mapsforeurope.org/licence)

### Get `Altitude (m)` {#get-altitude}

`terra::extract()` returns the value of the raster at each plot, in a column
named after the raster layer, here `eurodem`. Any elevation raster in meters
works the same way, for example a national elevation model; use its layer name
in place of `eurodem`.

```{r}
data_sites <- data_sites |>
  mutate(
    "Altitude (m)" = terra::extract(altitude, terra::vect(data_sites))$eurodem
    )
data_sites
```

A plot outside the raster, or over the sea, gets `NA`. `resy_classify()`
evaluates a missing altitude as 0 m and warns with the number of such plots, so
a mountain plot without altitude can fail a rule such as "higher than 1000 m".
The same happens to all plots when the header table has no altitude column.
Check for missing values before classifying:

```{r altitude-na}
sum(is.na(data_sites$`Altitude (m)`))
```

### Add `Altitude (m)` to the header table

`resy_classify()` reads the altitude from the header table, which has one row
per plot. Dropping the geometry from `data_sites` gives such a table. If you
already have a header table, join the new column to it by `PlotObservationID`.

```{r header}
header <- sf::st_drop_geometry(data_sites)
head(header)
```

## Crop your own altitude data

Download EuroDEM (European Digital Elevation Model), an elevation map of Europe by EuroGeographics, co-funded by the European Union, from <https://www.mapsforeurope.org/datasets/euro-dem>.

The code in this section needs the downloaded file, so it is not run when this vignette is built.

### Load altitude data

Save EuroDEM data in the data folder of your R project. From there, you can load the raster file.

```{r eurodem-data, eval = FALSE}
altitude <- terra::rast(
  here::here("data", "euro-dem-tif", "data", "eurodem.tif")
)
```

EuroDEM stores its extent in arcseconds; dividing by 3600 converts it to degrees.

```{r transform-eurodem-data, eval = FALSE}
e <- terra::ext(altitude)
terra::ext(altitude) <- terra::ext(
  e[1] / 3600, e[2] / 3600, e[3] / 3600, e[4] / 3600
)
```

The altitude data needs the right coordinate reference system: EPSG:4258, ETRS89 (European Terrestrial Reference System 1989) in degrees.

```{r assign-epsg-to-eurodem, eval = FALSE}
terra::crs(altitude) <- "EPSG:4258"  # geographic ETRS89, degrees
```

Get an overview of the status of the EuroDEM data.

```{r overview-of-eurodem, eval = FALSE}
altitude
```

### Load your sites

Load your sites data, with the columns `PlotObservationID`, `Longitude` and `Latitude`, transform it to an sf object and align its coordinate reference system with the altitude raster.

```{r load-data-sites, eval = FALSE}
data_sites <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "data_sites.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(altitude))
```

### Crop to your area

Crop the elevation map to the area covered by your vegetation relevés:

```{r crop-data, eval = FALSE}
altitude_cropped <- data_sites |>
  sf::st_buffer(0.5) |> # degrees now, ~50 km
  sf::st_bbox() |>
  terra::crop(x = altitude, y = _) |>
  terra::project("EPSG:4326")
```

Save the cropped and therefore smaller altitude data for later use.

```{r write-raster, eval = FALSE}
terra::writeRaster(
  altitude_cropped,
  here::here("data", "data_altitude.tif"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

Now you can go on with the above [example](#example) and [get altitude data](#get-altitude), loading `data_altitude.tif` in place of the example file.
